§ 2Content

REPRODUCTION

  1. 6. Vegetative Propagation
  • It is a process of asexual reproduction in which a new plant grows from the vegetative parts of the parent plant, such as the root, stem, or leaf. It can also occur through cutting or grafting parts of the plant.
  • This method does not involve seeds, and the new plant is genetically identical to the parent.
The buds in potato are called "eyes", they are axillary buds located at the nodes of stem. These eyes can grow into a new potato plant.

Types of Vegetative Propagation:

  • (a) Cutting: A part of plant (stem or leaf) is cut and planted into the soil. E.g. Rose plant, money plant, banana plant, sugarcane plant.
  • (b) Layering: The stem of the plant is bent to the ground and covered with soil. E.g. Lemon, strawberry.
  • (c) Grafting: Cutting from some other plant attached to the stem of the plant and planted into the soil. E.g. Rose plant.

Vegetative propagation diagram: Cutting (cut, Rooting hormone), Grafting, Layering, Isolated cells → Explant → Tissue culture → Inoculated cells → A small cell can form a whole plant

  1. 7. Tissue Culture
  • Tissue culture is a modern method of asexual reproduction used to grow new plants from a small group of cells or tissues in a laboratory under sterile conditions. E.g. Tissue culture is widely used in ornamental plant like snake plant. Cost of such plants are very high.
  1. 8. Spore Formation
  • It is a process of asexual reproduction in which an organism produces spores → tiny, usually single-celled structures, that can grow into new individuals under favorable conditions. E.g. Spore formation in Rhizopus (bread mould) a type of fungi.

§ 3SEXUAL REPRODUCTION IN PLANTS

  • Sexual reproduction in plants involves the fusion of male and female gametes (pollen and ovule) to form a zygote, which develops into a seed that grows into a new plant.
  • This process occurs through flowers, the reproductive organs of plants.

Types of Flowers

  1. 1. Bisexual Flowers (Hermaphrodite Flowers)
  • These flowers contain both male (stamens) and female (pistil) reproductive organs in the same flower.
  • They are capable of self-pollination as well as cross-pollination. E.g. Hibiscus, mustard, lily, sunflower.
  1. 2. Unisexual Flowers
  • These flowers contain only one reproductive organ → either stamens or pistil, but not both.
  • They are capable of cross-pollination. E.g. Male flower that only has only stamens → Corn, Cucumber, Female flower that only has carpels → Papaya, watermelon.

→ Monoecious Plants: Male and female reproductive parts are present on the same plant. E.g. Maize, cucumber.

→ Dioecious Plants: Male and female reproductive parts are present on separate plants.

  • E.g. Papaya, date palm.

Anatomy of a Flower

  • Male reproductive part (collectively called Stamen) consists of:
  • → Filament: Supports anther.
  • → Anther: Produces pollen (yellow colour).
  • Female reproductive part (collectively called Pistil) consists of:
  • → Stigma: Sticky bulb that catches pollen.
  • → Style: Passageway for pollen.

REPRODUCTION

  • → Ovary: The part of pistil that holds the eggs awaiting fertilization and later becomes the fruit.
  • Isogamy: Fusion of morphologically similar gametes (same size and shape). E.g. Chlamydomonas.
  • Anisogamy: Fusion of morphologically dissimilar gametes (different size and shape). E.g. Some algae, fungi.
  • Oogamy: A type of anisogamy where large, non-motile egg fuses with small, motile sperm. E.g. humans.

Pollination

  • Pollination is the process where pollen, containing a plant's male reproductive cells, is transferred to the female part of a plant (stigma). This transfer is essential for plant reproduction, leading to fertilization and the development of seeds.

Types of Pollination:

  1. 1. Self-Pollination (Autogamy)
  • Pollen from anther is transferred to the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant.
  • No genetic variation. E.g. Pea, tomato.
  1. 2. Cross-Pollination (Allogamy)
  • Pollen is transferred from the anther of one flower to the stigma of another flower on a different plant of the same species.
  • Promotes genetic diversity. E.g. Apple, sunflower.
AgentType of PollinationExamples
InsectEntomophilyRose, Lotus
WindAnemophilyMaize, Grass
WaterHydrophilyVallisneria
  • After pollination, the pollen grain germinates on the stigma and forms a pollen tube that carries the male gamete to the ovule in the ovary. Male and female gametes fuse to form the Zygote. Zygote develops into an embryo. The ovule becomes seed and ovary becomes fruit.

Specific Terms Associated

False Fruit

  • A fruit that develops from other parts of a flower, in addition to ovary, and does not require fertilisation. In this type of fertilization, thallus is also involved. E.g. Apple, cashew nut.

Parthenocarpic Fruits

  • They are seedless fruits, that develops without fertilisation of an ovule. E.g. Banana, grape, cucumber.

Drupe Fruit

  • It is a type of fruit with a hard shell that includes a seed and has an inner flesh. E.g. Coconut.

§ 4HUMAN REPRODUCTIVE SYSTEM

Parts of Male Reproductive System

  1. 1. Testes
  • It is located in the scrotum (a sac outside the body to keep sperm cool).
  • It produces sperm and testosterone (male sex hormone).
  • Sperm production in males typically begin around the age of 10-12 yrs.
  1. 2. Vas Deferens (Sperm Duct)
  • Tube that transports mature sperm from epididymis to urethra.
  1. 3. Seminal Vesicles and Prostate Gland
  • It adds seminal fluid to sperm to form semen.
  • Semen provides nutrients and a medium for sperm to swim.
  1. 4. Urethra
  • It carries semen and urine, but never at the same time.
  • It passes through the penis and exits the body.

Parts of Female Reproductive System

  1. 1. Ovaries (primary sex organ in females)
  • Ovaries produce eggs (ova) and estrogen + progesterone (female sex hormones).
  • A female is born with all the egg cells (oocytes) she will ever have. At the age of 12, the ovaries start to mature.
  1. 2. Fallopian Tubes (Oviducts)
  • The site where sperm meet egg and fertilization occurs. The cilia inside the fallopian tubes push the egg towards the uterus.
  1. 3. Uterus (Womb)
  • Muscular organ where a fertilized egg implants and develops into a foetus. The innermost lining of the uterus is called endometrium.

REPRODUCTION

  1. 4. Cervix
  • The cervix is the lower part of the uterus that connects to the vagina. During childbirth, it must open to allow the baby to pass through.
Thickening of uterine wall for preparation for potential implantation of fertilised egg during pregnancy. When pregnancy does not occur after the uterine lining thickens, the lining is shed through menstruation.
Cervical cancer is caused by: HPV (Human Papilloma Virus).

Menopause

  • Menopause is the permanent cessation of menstruation in women, marking the end of their reproductive years. It typically occurs in the late 40s to early 50s, with the average age being around 51. This stage is characterized by the ovaries no longer releasing eggs and a decrease in the production of estrogen and progesterone.

Fertilization

  • Fertilization is the process where a male gamete (sperm) and a female gamete (egg) fuse to form a zygote, which is the first cell of a new individual.

Types of Fertilisation

  1. 1. Internal Fertilisation: The process of a sperm cell and an egg cell fusing inside the female body during reproduction. E.g. In humans.
  2. 2. External Fertilisation: A reproductive process where a male sperm fertilises a female's egg outside of the female's body. E.g. Frog, earthworms, crab.
  • Viviparous: Animals that develop inside the parent's body and give birth to live offspring. E.g. Cats, dogs, humans.
  • Ovoviviparous: Animals that lay eggs and the eggs develop inside mother's body. E.g. Sharks, snakes, some fishes (like guppies).
  • Oviparous: Animals that lay eggs and the eggs develop outside the mother's body. E.g. Birds, frogs, lizards. (Exception: Platypus is the only mammal reproduced oviparously).

Process of Fertilization

Process involved:

  1. 1. Gametogenesis: This is the process of forming gametes → Sperm in males and eggs in females, essential for reproduction.
  1. 2. Insemination: It involves the transfer of sperm into the female reproductive tract during intercourse.
  1. 3. Fertilisation: The sperm meets and fuses with the egg, forming a zygote (the first cell of the new baby).
  1. 4. Implantation: The zygote develops into a blastocyst and attaches itself to the uterine wall, beginning pregnancy.
  1. 5. Gestation: This is the period of development where the embryo grows and forms into a foetus inside the uterus.
  1. 6. Parturition: The final stage, where the baby is delivered through childbirth.

Role of Arteries and Veins in Pregnancy

During pregnancy:

  • Arteries in the uterus (especially the spiral arteries) supply oxygen-rich blood and nutrients to the placenta, supporting the growing fetus.
  • Veins carry deoxygenated blood and waste products from the placenta back to the mother's circulation for disposal.

Fetus diagram: Umbilical cord, Fetus, Uterus, Placenta, Umbilical cord, Wharton's Jelly, Umbilical vein, Umbilical arteries

Totipotency

  • It is the ability of a single cell to produce a fertile, adult individual.

In-Vitro Fertilisation (IVF)

  • In in-vitro fertilisation (IVF), an egg is combined with a sperm outside the mother's body, in a laboratory setting.

Parthenogenesis

  • A type of asexual reproduction, where an organism develops from an unfertilised egg, without the need for sperm. The unfertilised egg completely develops into a new organism. E.g. Honey bees, lizards.

REPRODUCTION

Metamorphosis in Butterfly

Butterfly metamorphosis is a complete transformation involving four distinct stages: Egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa (chrysalis), and adult butterfly.

DIGESTION AND RESPIRATION

§ 6DIGESTIVE SYSTEM

Digestion

  • Digestion is the process of breaking down food into simpler substances so the body can absorb and use the nutrients.

Main Organs of Digestive System

Mouth (Oral Cavity/Buccal Cavity)

  • Digestion starts here. Teeth chew the food (mechanical digestion).
  • Saliva (from salivary glands) contains salivary amylase, which breaks down starch (complex carbohydrates to simple carbohydrates).
  • Tongue helps in mixing food and swallowing.

Pharynx and Oesophagus

  • Pharynx connects mouth to esophagus.
  • Oesophagus (length: 25 cm) is a muscular tube that pushes food to the stomach through peristalsis (wave-like movement).

Stomach

  • J-shaped muscular organ.

Secretes:

  • Hydrochloric acid (HCl): Kills germs and provides acidic medium. HCl is present in gastric juice (pH: 1.6).
  • Pepsin: Digests proteins (works in acidic medium only).
  • Mucus: Protects the delicate stomach lining from acid.

Sphincter Muscle

  • It allows food to pass from stomach to small intestine.

Small Intestine

  • It is the longest part of the alimentary canal (6.5 to 7.5 meters). It is the main site of digestion and absorption.
  • It is divided into three parts: duodenum, jejunum, ileum.

Digestive Juices Received in Small Intestines from Liver

Bile (bile juice)

  • Bile juice is stored in gall bladder and released by liver.
  • Bile is not an enzyme but plays a crucial supporting role in digestion.
Maltase enzyme in small intestine converts Maltose to Glucose.

Function of Bile:

  • Bile is alkaline (basic) in nature.
  • It neutralizes the acidic food before it enters the small intestine.
  • This creates a favorable pH for the action of pancreatic and intestinal enzymes.

Emulsification of Fats:

  • Bile breaks down large fat globules into smaller globules. This process is called emulsification.

Pancreas

  • Function: Digests carbs, proteins, and fats.
  • Pancreas release pancreatic juice:
  • → Amylase: Breaks down carbs.
  • → Lipase: Breaks down fats into fatty acids and glycerol.
  • → Trypsin (works in basic medium): Breaks down proteins into amino acids.
Roughage found in:
- Green leafy vegetables, Fruits, etc.
- Fibre: Promotes peristalsis

Large Intestine

  • Length: 1.5 m.
  • Function: Absorbs water and electrolytes from the remaining undigested food, solidifying it into feces for elimination.
  • Large intestine comprises of:
  • → Cecum: First part of the large intestine, and it connects the small intestine to the colon.
  • → Colon: Responsible for absorbing water from indigestible food residues.

Liver

  • The study of the liver is called Hepatology.
  • The liver is the largest gland in the human body.
  • It is located on the right side of the abdomen and is dark red-brown in color.

Functions of the Liver:

  • It converts glucose into glycogen for storage (process known as glycogenesis).
  • It converts amino acids into proteins (vital for growth and repair).
  • It stores glycogen in liver cells to maintain blood sugar levels.

Important Liver Cells:

  1. 1. Kupffer Cells
  • Star-shaped phagocytic cells found in the lining of liver sinusoids.
  • Functions:
  • They are involved in the breakdown of RBCs.
  • They are clean pathogens and debris from the blood.
  • Kupffer cells have regenerative ability
